# gositter vs C tree-sitter 0.25.0

Ratios are gositter divided by the other side: below 1.00 means gositter is better. `min` is the fastest timed pass over all rounds, `med` the median pass. The headline time columns are min-pass wall and user+sys CPU; median wall is secondary because it moves with the load on the machine. `CPU/wall` (sum of user+sys over sum of wall) is the number of logical CPUs the process got: a j=all cell under 0.7 x j is marked `*`, its wall is load noise and only CPU, instructions and cycles count there. Wall and CPU are per pass over the whole list; CPU, instructions and cycles are process-wide and count all threads, including the Go GC. Peak columns are the maximum over the processes of that config. A matrix process runs 6 passes (warm-up included) and the gositter peak at j=all still grows at that point, so the matrix peaks are labelled `after 6 passes`; the memory numbers for the steady state are the `steady` ones, from one process of 41 passes per grammar, set, j and side (`run.py mem`). 3 significant digits.

### Machine

From `bin/BUILDINFO.txt`:

    built: 2026-10-13T08:33:09Z
    host: Linux 7.0.0-30-generic x86_64, AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D 8-Core Processor, 16 cpus
    glibc: glibc 2.36
    topology: 1 socket x 8 cores x 2 threads, smt active 1
    governor: powersave
    cpufreq driver: amd-pstate-epp, epp balance_performance
    cgroup cpu.max: max 100000
    perf_event_paranoid: 4
    go: go version go1.27.2 linux/amd64
    cc: gcc = gcc (Debian 12.2.0-14+deb12u1) 12.2.0
    cc default pic/pie macros: #define __pie__ 2 #define __pic__ 2 #define __PIC__ 2 #define __PIE__ 2 
    tree-sitter runtime: go-tree-sitter v0.25.0 src/lib.c, sha256 of src/*.c src/*.h concatenated: dbe269413058b1685fd699115a4f45af29fead6950466c4f1a0c8f0e1be7c19b

Linux measures. Instructions and cycles are perf_event_open hardware counters, user mode only, of all threads (one inherited event per thread that exists when counting starts). Counting starts at the first line of main (C) or at package init (Go), not at exec; a 0 means perf_event_open was refused. That is right for a timed pass but not for a whole process: it leaves out the loader, the Go runtime start and all kernel work, and what is left out differs per side. So the cost of a first-parse process is in the `exec to exit` rows: each of these processes runs under `perf stat`, which counts user and kernel mode from exec to exit, and has its own counters switched off (BENCH_NOPERF), because the two sets together need more hardware counters than are free and perf would then scale its counts. Results from before that change have the in-process counts, as `user instr after main/init` and `user cycles after main/init`. `start to main` is not measured (n/a). `peak RSS` and `peak footprint` are both VmHWM of /proc/self/status, the peak resident set, so the two columns are equal here. ru_maxrss is not used: on Linux it keeps the peak of the process image before exec (the watchdog's python, about 10 MB), which is a floor under every small process. `RSS above loaded` is VmHWM minus VmRSS after the files were read. All Go sides are built without cgo for the counters; gsbench is the CGO_ENABLED=0 build.

RSS on Linux and on macOS is not the same measure: the two kernels count shared, file-backed and compressed pages differently, the allocators differ (glibc malloc against the macOS zone allocator) and so does the page size (4 KB on amd64, 16 KB on Apple silicon). Compare memory only between sides on one machine, never across the two.

C is `cbench` at -O2 -std=c11, the best stock C build. These are not all the flags cgo uses here: on Linux cgo adds -fPIC (and -m64 -pthread) to every C file, while `cbench` is the gcc default, PIE, and with gcc -fPIC stops the inlining of exported functions in lib.c. C-pic is `cbench` with -fPIC on lib.c and the grammars (one round, parse and cursor only): C-pic against C is the cost of that flag, cgo against C-pic the cost of the binding. Both are printed under the summary. C-O3 is the same sources at -O3, the default of the upstream tree-sitter Makefile; it runs parse and cursor only. C-nopragma is C with one source line removed, see below. C-clang, where it ran, is C built by clang instead of the compiler cgo uses (one round, parse and cursor only): it shows how much of the result is the C compiler. Exact flags: `bin/BUILDINFO.txt`, `bin/BUILDINFO-O3.txt` and `bin/BUILDINFO-clang.txt`.

`walk` and `cursor` rows time the parse plus the traversal of each tree. The `walk minus parse` and `cursor minus parse` rows are the traversal alone: min pass of the walk or cursor process minus min pass of the parse process of the same grammar, set, j and side. They are a difference of two processes, so small ones are noisy; a difference at or below zero prints n/a.

### What each side pays

Pure C (`C`, `C-O3`) is the baseline for the speed of the runtime. The cgo side measures the go-tree-sitter binding, not the C runtime.

- Optimisation pragma. The pinned parser.c of 8 grammars (bash, c, cpp, csharp, julia, kotlin, ruby, verilog) carries the line `#pragma clang optimize off` (for GCC: `#pragma GCC optimize ("O0")`), so the compiler builds the lexer and the tables of these grammars without optimisation at any -O level. That holds for `C`, `C-O3` and cgo alike, and it is how upstream ships these grammars, so the stock build stays the baseline. `C-nopragma` is `C` (-O2, same lib.o, same scanner objects) with only that line removed from these 8 parser.c; it runs for these grammars only, for the others it would be `C`. gositter has no such switch: its tables and lexers are compiled like the rest of the Go code.
- Tree lifetime. A gositter tree lives in slabs owned by its parser and is valid only until the next Parse, Reset or SetLanguage on that parser; `Tree.Close` is a no-op. A C tree is owned by the caller and the runtime pays malloc and free per subtree for that. This harness keeps one live tree per parser and frees it at the next parse, which is the only lifetime gositter supports and its best case. C has no such reuse, by design of the library.
- cgo binding. go-tree-sitter v0.25.0 routes every C malloc, calloc, realloc and free through a Go callback (its `init` calls `ts_set_allocator`), `Kind()` copies the name with `C.GoString`, `Child()` and the cursor's `Node()` allocate a `*Node` on the Go heap, and `Parser.Parse` reads the source through a callback that copies the rest of the source (`C.CString(text[i:])`) at each call and frees the copies when the parse ends. One 100 KB scala file needs about 950 MB that way against 11 MB in pure C, so a cgo config can end in KILL_RSS. That is a memory result of the cgo side, not a missing measurement: its cells print KILL_RSS, the config is listed under `Configs a side did not finish` with the RSS of the other sides, and it is absent from the cgo ratios (the summary prints the n of each cell).
  With glibc the freed copies stay in the malloc arena of the thread that made them, so at j above 1 the cgo RSS grows over the passes as a large file moves between threads. Measured here on one 45 KB scala file alone, j=16: 335 MB after 2 passes, 652 MB after 6, killed above 1024 MB before 21; 375 MB after 41 passes with `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=1`, which no run of this report sets. The largest scala file needs 806 MB alone, so the cgo scala cells at j=all can be KILL_RSS at a cap well above that.
- Child(i) walk. `ts_node_child` scans from the first child on each call, so the `walk` rows are not the usual C traversal; `cursor` (TreeCursor) is.

Malloc* and GO* variables seen by the benchmark processes: `{'GOTOOLCHAIN': 'local', 'GOPATH': '/go', 'GOLANG_VERSION': '1.27.2'}`.

1-minute load average at the end of each matrix process: min 1.41, median 3.16, max 20.

## Cross-side agreement

For every walk and cursor config the node count of each pass and the checksum of the last pass (per node: first byte of the kind + start byte + end byte, summed over the list) of each side that finished are compared with gositter. Parse configs visit no node; their error-file counts are in the table above.

Nodes and checksum agree: yes, in all 244 walk and cursor configs (cgo in 238, C in 244, C-nopragma in 92, C-O3 in 122, C-clang in 122, C-pic in 122 compared with gositter).

## Configs a side did not finish: 28

A process killed by the watchdog at its memory cap (KILL_RSS) or time limit (KILL_TIME). This is a result of that side, not a missing measurement: with `side` cgo the go-tree-sitter binding needed more memory than the cap for a list that gositter and pure C parsed with the peak RSS in the last two columns. `cmp` is the oracle, which holds the C tree through go-tree-sitter next to the gositter tree: a KILL_RSS there is cgo-side memory too and says nothing about the trees, which stay uncompared for that list. The per-grammar tables print the status in the cell of that side, and the config is absent from its ratios.

## Summary across grammars

Each cell: geometric mean (min-max) of the per-grammar ratio, and n = the number of grammars in that cell (a grammar whose process was killed on one side is missing from the cell, see `Configs a side did not finish`; the C-nopragma cells hold only the 8 grammars with the pragma). CPU, instructions and cycles use the median pass. `walk` and `cursor` include the parse; the second table of each side is the traversal alone, from min passes.

A list under 100000 bytes is left out of every cell here: one pass over it takes well under a millisecond, so its numbers, above all at j=all, are thread wake-up and scheduler cost and not parsing. Its per-grammar tables are still printed, with the set marked `too small`. Left out: java realerr (907 B), javascript realerr (1898 B), lua realerr (291 B), php realerr (25 B), python realerr (982 B), rust realerr (257 B).

613 of 978 side-configs at j above 1 got under 0.7 x j logical CPUs (CPU/wall): the wall columns of the j=all rows are valid only where that count is 0, CPU and cycles are the j=all numbers otherwise.

j=all is 16 threads on 1 socket x 8 cores x 2 threads, smt active 1, the same for every side. With SMT that is two threads per physical core, so a j=all wall is not a one-thread-per-core number. In this run the j=1 min-pass wall is 6.68x (1.22-9.84) the j=all one and a j=all pass costs 1.47x (1.03-1.67) the cycles of a j=1 pass: median (range) over 888 side-configs.

### bash: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 1.43 (real), 2 (realerr), 1.39 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| real | cold | 1.73 | 15800 | 7.66 | 728 | 68200 | 728 | 68200 | 0.00237 |
| real | steady | 1.43 | 3320 | 7.64 | 728 | 67900 | 728 | 67900 | 0.00197 |
| realerr | cold | 20.1 | 181000 | 8.81 | 3270 | 316000 | 3270 | 316000 | 0.00614 |
| realerr | steady | 2 | 135 | 10.3 | 3270 | 314000 | 3270 | 314000 | 0.000613 |
| broken | cold | 5.71 | 139000 | 8.3 | 2480 | 290000 | 2480 | 290000 | 0.0023 |
| broken | steady | 1.39 | 33500 | 8.29 | 2480 | 290000 | 2480 | 290000 | 0.000561 |

### bash: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### c: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 0.0598 (real), 0.113 (realerr), 0.0594 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |

| real | steady | 0.0598 | 8620 | 7.04 | 1430 | 136000 | 1430 | 136000 | 0 |
| realerr | cold | 3.27 | 54500 | 7.35 | 5040 | 478000 | 5040 | 478000 | 0.000649 |

| broken | steady | 0.0594 | 16600 | 7.87 | 4090 | 475000 | 4090 | 475000 | 0 |

### c: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### cpp: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 1.09 (real), 1.34 (realerr), 1.12 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |

### cpp: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### csharp: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 1.08 (real), 1.67 (realerr), 1.11 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

### csharp: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### golang: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 0.0396 (real), 0.767 (realerr), 0.0818 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| real | cold | 0.137 | 15500 | 7.01 | 1990 | 186000 | 1990 | 186000 | 0 |
| real | steady | 0.0396 | 8690 | 7.01 | 1990 | 186000 | 1990 | 186000 | 0 |
| realerr | cold | 6.03 | 189000 | 7.23 | 5570 | 532000 | 5570 | 532000 | 0.00108 |
| realerr | steady | 0.767 | 69000 | 7.27 | 5560 | 531000 | 5560 | 531000 | 0.000138 |
| broken | cold | 3.04 | 90700 | 7.5 | 3600 | 385000 | 3600 | 385000 | 0.000845 |
| broken | steady | 0.0818 | 25200 | 7.51 | 3600 | 385000 | 3600 | 385000 | 0 |

### golang: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

| #0 2052 B | init+parse1 ms | 0.182 | 0.249 | 0.18 | 0.729 | 1.01 | 15 |

### hcl: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 2.36 (real), 5.91 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| real | cold | 2.43 | 5220 | 7.02 | 2600 | 245000 | 2600 | 245000 | 0.000935 |
| real | steady | 2.36 | 1560 | 7.01 | 2600 | 245000 | 2600 | 245000 | 0.000907 |
| broken | cold | 6.95 | 19600 | 7.67 | 3840 | 389000 | 3840 | 389000 | 0.00181 |
| broken | steady | 5.91 | 4820 | 7.53 | 3840 | 389000 | 3840 | 389000 | 0.00154 |

### hcl: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### java: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 0.012 (real), 4.5 (realerr), 0.106 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| real | cold | 0.0821 | 4300 | 7.01 | 1200 | 112000 | 1200 | 112000 | 0 |
| real | steady | 0.012 | 1390 | 7.01 | 1200 | 112000 | 1200 | 112000 | 0 |
| realerr | cold | 26.5 | 86600 | 12.5 | 172 | 18700 | 172 | 18700 | 0.154 |
| realerr | steady | 4.5 | 104 | 11.5 | 152 | 13800 | 152 | 13800 | 0.0296 |
| broken | cold | 2.46 | 106000 | 7.9 | 2770 | 305000 | 2770 | 305000 | 0.00089 |
| broken | steady | 0.106 | 21300 | 7.88 | 2770 | 305000 | 2770 | 305000 | 0 |

### java: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### javascript: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 0.0603 (real), 1 (realerr), 0.112 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| real | cold | 0.176 | 23600 | 8.22 | 2160 | 203000 | 2160 | 203000 | 0 |
| real | steady | 0.0603 | 15500 | 8.22 | 2160 | 203000 | 2160 | 203000 | 0 |
| realerr | cold | 16.4 | 20900 | 9.89 | 97.7 | 9360 | 97.7 | 9360 | 0.168 |
| realerr | steady | 1 | 23.1 | 9.78 | 95 | 8760 | 95 | 8760 | 0.0105 |
| broken | cold | 2.74 | 164000 | 8.55 | 5060 | 586000 | 5060 | 586000 | 0.000542 |
| broken | steady | 0.112 | 45400 | 8.53 | 5060 | 585000 | 5060 | 585000 | 0 |

### javascript: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### json: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 0.123 (real), 0.289 (realerr), 0.112 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| real | cold | 0.237 | 35900 | 7 | 1880 | 186000 | 1880 | 186000 | 0.000126 |
| real | steady | 0.123 | 28800 | 6.99 | 1880 | 186000 | 1880 | 186000 | 0 |
| realerr | cold | 2.39 | 13500 | 8 | 681 | 86000 | 681 | 86000 | 0.00352 |
| realerr | steady | 0.289 | 59.8 | 7.95 | 680 | 85500 | 680 | 85500 | 0.000426 |
| broken | cold | 0.721 | 91500 | 7.36 | 2750 | 317000 | 2750 | 317000 | 0.000262 |
| broken | steady | 0.112 | 29300 | 7.34 | 2750 | 317000 | 2750 | 317000 | 0 |

### json: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### julia: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 0.183 (real), 1.26 (realerr), 0.114 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| real | steady | 0.183 | 46300 | 7.1 | 5350 | 488000 | 5350 | 488000 | 0 |
| realerr | cold | 32 | 962000 | 27.2 | 21500 | 1970000 | 21500 | 1970000 | 0.00149 |
| realerr | steady | 1.26 | 186000 | 23.7 | 21500 | 1970000 | 21500 | 1970000 | 0 |
| broken | cold | 7.16 | 55800 | 18.8 | 5650 | 532000 | 5650 | 532000 | 0.00127 |
| broken | steady | 0.114 | 21200 | 18.7 | 5650 | 532000 | 5650 | 532000 | 0 |

### julia: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### kotlin: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 0.0251 (real), 0.76 (realerr), 0.0345 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |

| real | steady | 0.0251 | 1420 | 11.2 | 1390 | 127000 | 1390 | 127000 | 0 |
| realerr | cold | 20.7 | 227000 | 14.3 | 3780 | 352000 | 3780 | 352000 | 0.00548 |
| realerr | steady | 0.76 | 457 | 14.3 | 3780 | 352000 | 3780 | 352000 | 0.000201 |

### kotlin: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### lua: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 1.03 (real), 10 (realerr), 1.09 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| real | cold | 1.09 | 8340 | 8 | 2030 | 190000 | 2030 | 190000 | 0.000535 |
| real | steady | 1.03 | 4500 | 8 | 2030 | 190000 | 2030 | 190000 | 0.000506 |
| realerr | cold | 78 | 173000 | 22 | 100 | 14500 | 100 | 14500 | 0.78 |
| realerr | steady | 10 | 224 | 20 | 64 | 5850 | 64 | 5850 | 0.156 |
| broken | cold | 2.82 | 80200 | 23.3 | 2600 | 297000 | 2600 | 297000 | 0.00108 |
| broken | steady | 1.09 | 16800 | 23.3 | 2600 | 296000 | 2600 | 296000 | 0.00042 |

### lua: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### php: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 3.46 (real), 10 (realerr), 4.85 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| real | cold | 3.6 | 27500 | 7 | 2380 | 217000 | 2380 | 217000 | 0.00151 |
| real | steady | 3.46 | 14000 | 7.01 | 2380 | 217000 | 2380 | 217000 | 0.00145 |
| realerr | cold | 41 | 170000 | 17 | 29 | 3140 | 29 | 3140 | 1.41 |
| realerr | steady | 10 | 240 | 15 | 22 | 1690 | 22 | 1690 | 0.455 |
| broken | cold | 8.49 | 70400 | 7.67 | 3890 | 399000 | 3890 | 399000 | 0.00218 |
| broken | steady | 4.85 | 21600 | 7.67 | 3890 | 399000 | 3890 | 399000 | 0.00125 |

### php: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### python: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 3.44 (real), 5.67 (realerr), 3.46 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| real | cold | 3.59 | 28200 | 9.21 | 3450 | 316000 | 3450 | 316000 | 0.00104 |
| real | steady | 3.44 | 18400 | 9.21 | 3450 | 316000 | 3450 | 316000 | 0.000996 |
| realerr | cold | 36.3 | 59300 | 11.3 | 137 | 13200 | 137 | 13200 | 0.265 |
| realerr | steady | 5.67 | 149 | 10.7 | 129 | 11500 | 129 | 11500 | 0.044 |
| broken | cold | 7.91 | 112000 | 9.29 | 5140 | 580000 | 5140 | 580000 | 0.00154 |
| broken | steady | 3.46 | 24900 | 9.28 | 5140 | 579000 | 5140 | 579000 | 0.000672 |

### python: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### ruby: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 2.17 (real), 2.33 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| real | cold | 2.26 | 11100 | 9.01 | 2270 | 209000 | 2270 | 209000 | 0.000998 |
| real | steady | 2.17 | 4220 | 9.01 | 2270 | 209000 | 2270 | 209000 | 0.000956 |
| broken | cold | 8.69 | 167000 | 9.57 | 4630 | 516000 | 4630 | 516000 | 0.00188 |
| broken | steady | 2.33 | 33600 | 9.55 | 4630 | 516000 | 4630 | 516000 | 0.000502 |

### ruby: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### rust: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 1.02 (real), 10 (realerr), 1.1 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| real | cold | 1.13 | 9880 | 8.02 | 2570 | 248000 | 2570 | 248000 | 0.000439 |
| real | steady | 1.02 | 2000 | 8.01 | 2570 | 248000 | 2570 | 248000 | 0.000397 |
| realerr | cold | 55 | 171000 | 18 | 258 | 26100 | 258 | 26100 | 0.213 |
| realerr | steady | 10 | 224 | 16 | 237 | 21400 | 237 | 21400 | 0.0422 |
| broken | cold | 5.71 | 109000 | 8.45 | 4330 | 494000 | 4330 | 494000 | 0.00132 |
| broken | steady | 1.1 | 25200 | 8.41 | 4330 | 493000 | 4330 | 493000 | 0.000254 |

### rust: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### scala: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 2.02 (real), 2.29 (realerr), 1.96 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| real | cold | 2.25 | 29300 | 446 | 3210 | 296000 | 3210 | 296000 | 0.000702 |
| real | steady | 2.02 | 5420 | 445 | 3210 | 295000 | 3210 | 295000 | 0.000629 |
| realerr | cold | 10.2 | 184000 | 725 | 5060 | 471000 | 5060 | 471000 | 0.00202 |
| realerr | steady | 2.29 | 81.2 | 723 | 5050 | 471000 | 5050 | 471000 | 0.000452 |
| broken | cold | 6.53 | 34700 | 379 | 3100 | 310000 | 3100 | 310000 | 0.0021 |
| broken | steady | 1.96 | 705 | 379 | 3100 | 310000 | 3100 | 310000 | 0.000631 |

### scala: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### tsx: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 0.0208 (real), 0.422 (realerr), 0.0563 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| real | cold | 0.299 | 8700 | 8.19 | 1100 | 103000 | 1100 | 103000 | 0.000272 |
| real | steady | 0.0208 | 32.7 | 8.18 | 1100 | 103000 | 1100 | 103000 | 0 |
| realerr | cold | 13.8 | 62100 | 8.58 | 1190 | 122000 | 1190 | 122000 | 0.0115 |
| realerr | steady | 0.422 | 188 | 8.56 | 1190 | 122000 | 1190 | 122000 | 0.000354 |
| broken | cold | 4 | 28500 | 8.34 | 1850 | 223000 | 1850 | 223000 | 0.00216 |
| broken | steady | 0.0563 | 4180 | 8.32 | 1850 | 222000 | 1850 | 222000 | 0 |

### tsx: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### typescript: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 0.065 (real), 0.232 (realerr), 0.118 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |

### typescript: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### verilog: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 0.0872 (real), 0.154 (realerr), 0.0664 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| real | steady | 0.0872 | 15.8 | 7.1 | 1210 | 110000 | 1210 | 110000 | 0 |
| realerr | cold | 6.46 | 60200 | 7.57 | 8940 | 1210000 | 8940 | 1210000 | 0.000722 |
| realerr | steady | 0.154 | 29200 | 7.58 | 8940 | 1210000 | 8940 | 1210000 | 0 |
| broken | cold | 5.84 | 49700 | 7.69 | 8350 | 1510000 | 8350 | 1510000 | 0.0007 |
| broken | steady | 0.0664 | 17300 | 7.69 | 8350 | 1510000 | 8350 | 1510000 | 0 |

### verilog: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

### zig: allocations per parse

`cold` is the first pass of a new parser (-warm 0), `steady` the pass after one warm-up pass over the same files. A gositter tree is valid only until the next Parse on its parser, which reuses the tree memory, so its steady count is what a re-parse still allocates: 0.203 (real), 2.27 (realerr), 0.0607 (broken) mallocs per parse here. A C tree is owned by the caller and every parse allocates it again. `gs new heap bytes` is Go TotalAlloc, new heap only, not the memory a parse uses; `C bytes` is the sum of the requested sizes. The two are not compared.

| set | parser | gs mallocs | gs new heap bytes | cgo Go mallocs | cgo C allocs | cgo C bytes | C allocs | C bytes | gs/C allocs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| real | cold | 0.66 | 94300 | 7.05 | 8000 | 737000 | 8000 | 737000 | 0 |
| real | steady | 0.203 | 59000 | 7.04 | 8000 | 737000 | 8000 | 737000 | 0 |
| realerr | cold | 19.1 | 758000 | 8.13 | 15900 | 1470000 | 15900 | 1470000 | 0.0012 |
| realerr | steady | 2.27 | 139000 | 7.93 | 15900 | 1470000 | 15900 | 1470000 | 0.000142 |
| broken | cold | 3.06 | 20200 | 7.62 | 7740 | 810000 | 7740 | 810000 | 0.000395 |
| broken | steady | 0.0607 | 4460 | 7.62 | 7740 | 810000 | 7740 | 810000 | 0 |

### zig: first parse in a new process (median of K processes)

`start to main` is process start to entry of main (gs-nocgo cannot read it), `init` is language + parser, `parse1` the first parse, `parse2` the second parse of the same file. `process user+sys` is getrusage after parse2. The `exec to exit` rows are `perf stat` on the whole process, user and kernel, both parses and the exit included: the cost of a new process. Any `after main/init` row is a user-mode count from the first line of main (C) or package init (Go) until after parse2 and leaves out the loader, the runtime start and the kernel.

## Cases where gositter is slower or uses more memory

Every ratio above 1.00 in this report, every input that gositter did not finish while the other side did, and every input killed on both sides. A killed process hit the memory or time cap of its run (`wd` in the last table); extreme inputs: time cap 30/120 s, memory cap 4096 MB. For an input killed on both sides the only comparison is the RSS peak the watchdog saw before the kill.
